# cutver 0.22.0-beta.1 — 27 November 2026

This is the beta of 0.22.0, one rung above `0.22.0-alpha.1`, and it is still a test version: the version
meant for real use is the final 0.22.0. The theme is the end of a release. A program driving cutver can
now read what the closing phase did as an object instead of scraping a table drawn for a person, and the
verdict files a release depends on now say which shape they are in.

Which part of this is new to you depends on where you are coming from, and the two answers are in the
first two sections.

- **Coming from 0.21.x or anything earlier**: two library changes break compatibility, and everything
  the alpha published — the channel ladder, resumable publications, the CI outputs, stable-only
  destinations — is new to you as well.
- **Coming from 0.22.0-alpha.1**: nothing breaks. Three commands gained a flag, one file gained a key,
  and one reported value was corrected in a flag that alpha.1 did not have.

If you use cutver to publish your own releases, this one affects you. If you write plugins or use cutver
as a library, the first section is yours.

## Breaking changes — if you are coming from 0.21.x or earlier

Two changes break compatibility, and both are library surfaces: the `cutver` crate used as a dependency.
The program on your PATH is unaffected by either.

**The plugin drivers now need to know which project folder they work in**
([#368](https://github.com/cutver/cutver/pull/368),
[c3b7390](https://github.com/cutver/cutver/commit/c3b7390da41ace1ca28d8d1331ee9653fbf6322c)).
`PluginManager::from_config` and `from_config_with_lookup` take a new parameter with the path to your
project, and `ProcessDriver::new` takes that path as its second argument.

*What to change*: pass the project path to either function. There is no version that works without it, and
that is on purpose. Before, the path was guessed from wherever the program happened to run, and a permission
granted over the wrong folder is a permission over files nobody chose.

**The steps that run before publishing changed shape**
([#363](https://github.com/cutver/cutver/pull/363),
[5050258](https://github.com/cutver/cutver/commit/50502580556660b2129d683d0111657a972eb53a)).
`cutver::preflight::run` takes a new parameter with the path to your project, and `run_supervised` now takes
the folder itself instead of a value that may be empty.

*What to change*: pass the path to `run`, and pass the folder (not an optional value) to `run_supervised`.
The optional value made it possible to skip supervision without saying so anywhere.

These are the two `0.22.0-alpha.1` recorded, and nothing in the range since that tag adds a third: the diff
against it touches no surface in `src/cli/args/` except by addition. Everything below adds flags, adds a key
to a file, or corrects one reported value.

## Coming from 0.22.0-alpha.1: nothing breaks

Three flags were added, one key was added to a file on disk, and one corrected value appears in a flag
that alpha.1 did not have. No flag, option or configuration key was removed or renamed between alpha.1
and this version.

- **The new flags** are `publish --json`, `attest --json` and `init --json`
  ([#408](https://github.com/cutver/cutver/pull/408)). Without the flag each command prints exactly what
  it printed in alpha.1, down to the byte: two goldens captured from the pre-change binary hold the
  dry-run tree and the published tree.
- **The attestation file** `cutver attest` writes now opens with `{"schemaVersion":1,`
  ([#412](https://github.com/cutver/cutver/pull/412)). If cutver is the reader — `publish --require-gate`,
  `plan --json` — you do nothing. If **you** parse that file, accept one more key at the front: a parser
  that refuses unknown fields rejects the files this version writes, and a parser that tolerates extras
  reads them unchanged. Files written by alpha.1 keep working, and their missing key means "the earlier
  shape", not "no record".
- **The corrected value** is `primary` in `init --update --json`, and alpha.1 had no `--json` on `init`
  at all, so nothing you could observe from alpha.1 changes ([#413](https://github.com/cutver/cutver/pull/413)).
  The detail is worth knowing if you write wrapping tooling: for a configuration whose first manifest is
  a `kind = "template"` sink and which names no source, `primary` is now the first manifest that is not
  a sink — the one the loader actually reads.

## What 0.22.0-alpha.1 brought, still here

The rest of the 0.22.0 line. It shipped in `0.22.0-alpha.1` and this version carries it unchanged, so it
is new only to readers arriving from 0.21.x.

### Test versions are now a channel

[#392](https://github.com/cutver/cutver/pull/392) · [#393](https://github.com/cutver/cutver/pull/393) ·
[ADR-0005](https://github.com/cutver/cutver/blob/main/docs/adr/0005-prerelease-channel-supersedes-0004.md#decision)

`cutver bump --channel alpha|beta|rc|stable` (and `plan`) publishes a version in a ladder. A named channel
adds its label and starts its counter, so `1.3.0` becomes `1.3.0-alpha.1`. If the version is already a test
version, the same flag **promotes** it: `--channel stable` on `1.2.0-rc.1` produces `1.2.0`, adding no
number.

This version is what that rule produces from `0.22.0-alpha.1`: `--channel beta` starts the beta counter
at `0.22.0-beta.1`.

The tool does not decide whether your version is "ready enough". It does not check the stages, so it
promotes an alpha exactly like an rc. That judgement is yours, and the program will not guess it.

If the request ends at the version the project already has, nothing is published: no commit, no tag, no
publish commands, and no plugin is called. A section says there were no changes, instead of reporting a
publication that did not happen.

One note on wording: the word "channel" on its own now always means this version ladder. The other two things
also called "channel" — the output for automation, and the record of authorizations — always carry their
full name so they cannot be confused with it.

### A publication can be continued instead of repeated

[#394](https://github.com/cutver/cutver/pull/394)

`cutver publish --resume --commit <sha>` picks up the last part of a publication that did not finish. It only
repeats steps that are safe to repeat: a tag already pointing at the right version, a push, the moving
major-version tag. It **refuses** to run a publish command unless a recorded authorization (an "attestation")
exists for that step and that exact version, and it tells you which step is missing by its position number.

There is a consequence worth understanding before you use it. That authorization **allows a step to run
again**. It does not record that the step already ran. If your package already went to the registry,
authorizing the step publishes it a second time. When the package is out and what is missing is the visible
part, the correct fix is to upload the files again and promote the release again — not to authorize a
continuation. [Publish ordering](https://github.com/cutver/cutver/blob/main/docs/internals/pipeline.md#publish-ordering)
explains both halves of this case.

The list of what a resume refuses moved out of the command reference in this version and lives with the
closing phase's rules: [resuming a closing phase](https://github.com/cutver/cutver/blob/main/docs/internals/release-resume.md).
No rule was dropped in the move.

### Automation now receives what was published

[#383](https://github.com/cutver/cutver/pull/383) · [#380](https://github.com/cutver/cutver/pull/380)

When cutver runs inside a CI system, it now reports what it published: the version, the channel, the tag and
the commit are available to the following steps. A workflow no longer needs to read a separate report file
to find out what happened.

The channel it reports is worked out from the version that was published, not from the flag someone passed.
If a version was promoted, it reports the stage it reached, which is the one that matters.

And with `--verbose`, when an external plugin writes error messages, you can see them. Before, a plugin that
failed quietly left you guessing.

### Where it gets published: only stable versions reach the distribution channels

[#399](https://github.com/cutver/cutver/pull/399) · [#398](https://github.com/cutver/cutver/pull/398)

This project had been distributing test versions as if they were stable. Not any more. The moving
major-version tag, the container tags (`latest`, `major`, `major.minor` and the commit identifier), Homebrew
and Scoop now receive **only stable versions**. When a test version skips one of those destinations, it says
so: a "stable only" section appears in the program output, and a notice names the destination it skipped.

The moving tag is the dangerous one. `uses: cutver/setup@v0` resolves by default to "the latest version", so
a tag that followed a test version would have handed an alpha to everyone who asked for the normal thing.
[Floating major tags](https://github.com/cutver/cutver/blob/main/docs/internals/pipeline.md#floating-major-tags-mechanics)
states the rule.

A test version is published, not withheld: `[publish].commands` still runs on every channel, so a crate
release on a prerelease channel reaches the registry under its own version number and stays out of the way
of anyone who did not name it.

The package managers also stopped offering a choice nobody could make correctly. `brew install
Row0902/tap/cutver` and `scoop install cutver` now install the version **with plugin support**, and
`cutver-plugins` stays for one more release as a deprecated bridge before it goes away
([installing cutver](https://github.com/cutver/cutver/blob/main/docs/guides/installation.md#installing-cutver)).
The lean version is still available as a release asset, for runners that download a binary directly.

## What is new in 0.22.0-beta.1

Four changes, and only the first is large.

### `publish`, `attest` and `init` answer on a machine surface

[#408](https://github.com/cutver/cutver/pull/408) ·
[#404](https://github.com/cutver/cutver/issues/404)

The end of a release was human-only output. A program driving cutver as a subprocess verified the tag with
`git ls-remote` — a second implementation of a check `publish` had just performed and refused on. Onboarding
a repository meant parsing a prose summary, and confirming the file a gate will read meant parsing another.

Each of the three commands now prints one compact object on one line, `schemaVersion` first, and a refusal
prints one envelope on stderr with nothing on stdout, so a consumer never reads half a document. The
refusal keeps stdout **empty** as an exact empty string — a stray newline fails the test that pins it.

**`publish --json`** reports what the closing phase did: `tag`, `commit`, `dry_run`, `tag_skipped`, the
`pushed_refs` git received, `floating_tag` and whether it moved, one entry per declared `[publish] commands`
with `position`, `command` and the `exit_code` its child returned, and the `on_post_release` outcome as
`dispatched` and `left_alone`. A wrapper reads each exit code here instead of scraping logs. `--dry-run`
reports the same keys with the values of a run that published nothing — empty `pushed_refs`, `null` exit
codes, `floating_tag_moved: false` — so an adapter parses one schema for a rehearsal and a real run.

**`attest --json`** reports the record it just wrote: `gate`, `commit`, `conclusion`, `verified_at`, `run`
(present and `null` when the gate named none, so the shape does not change) and `path`, spelled relative to
the workspace root — the file `publish --require-gate` reads. A wrapper confirms what it is about to rely on
instead of re-deriving the directory from the configuration.

**`init --json`** reports `manifests` — each with `path`, `is_root` and `kind` — the `primary` source of
truth and `files_written`. The `--update` branch reports the configuration it appended to, and `[]` when it
had nothing to append, so the object never claims a file the run did not write.

[The release tail's three surfaces](https://github.com/cutver/cutver/blob/main/docs/internals/machine-contract-release-tail.md)
state every key, in order, with what a consumer does with it. The keys are also pinned as a baseline in
`tests/schema_compat.rs`, which fails if `schemaVersion` moves or a key disappears, because field order is
part of the contract.

### The attestation file says which shape it is

[#412](https://github.com/cutver/cutver/pull/412) ·
[#409](https://github.com/cutver/cutver/issues/409)

The file `cutver attest` writes had no version key, so a consumer could not tell "no attestation for this
commit" from "an attestation in a shape I do not know". Both read as a refusal, because `publish
--require-gate` fails closed over a deliberately total parse — the worst failure this file can have, since
a gate would disable itself on a format change.

The record is now written through the envelope the other machine surfaces already use, so the file opens with
`{"schemaVersion":1,` and its value comes from the same constant the printed surfaces use, rather than a
second copy of the number. The record's own keys keep their order and nothing else about the file changes.

Compatibility is additive, and no reader has to do anything to upgrade. A file written before the key
existed keeps reading as the attestation it holds, so no recorded verdict becomes absent, and the absence
now means the earlier shape rather than an error. An end-to-end test proves a hand-written legacy record
still lets `publish --require-gate` release; another asserts that every `.json` file in a configured
`[gates]` dir opens with the version `--json` printed, so a writer that stopped adding it fails the suite.

### `init`'s reported primary source now agrees with the loader

[#413](https://github.com/cutver/cutver/pull/413) ·
[#410](https://github.com/cutver/cutver/issues/410)

`init --update` worked out the source of truth from the `toml_edit` document, and the loader worked it out
again in `deduce_current_source`. Nothing tied the two, and both answer with a path, so an ordering change
on one side would have left `primary` naming a manifest the release does not read, with no test failing.

A new equivalence test loads each fixture through the crate's own loader and requires both answers to name
the same manifest. The case it exposed is the behaviour change: for a configuration whose first manifest is
a `kind = "template"` sink and which names no source, `init --update --json` used to report the sink and now
reports the first non-sink manifest. A template sink generates its target from the version instead of
holding one, so it can never be the source — the old value was the defect.

Nothing else moved. The human summary never printed `primary`, the `--update` append path keeps its exact
output (so a declared sink is not appended twice), and the object keeps its three keys.

### This repository's pipeline records its smoke verdicts before publishing

[#406](https://github.com/cutver/cutver/pull/406)

The guarantee that the smoke matrix passed lived in the release workflow's `needs:` graph, where a
reordered job or a re-run of the publishing job alone can skip it. It now lives in a file `cutver publish`
verifies itself: this repository's `cutver.toml` declares `[gates] require = ["smoke", "smoke-plugins"]`,
an `attest` job records both verdicts for the release commit with the binary the smoke job already
exercised, and the publishing runner downloads them before `cutver publish` runs. The refusal names both
the commit being published and the commit the file covers.

For you, this is a worked example rather than a change: nothing in your configuration is affected unless
you declare `[gates]` yourself. The next release cut from `main` — this one — is the first that cannot
publish without the two verdicts recorded.

## Fixes

These shipped in `0.22.0-alpha.1`; nothing in this version changes them.

- **An error message recommended something the program itself refuses** ([#398](https://github.com/cutver/cutver/pull/398)):
  when a publish was rejected, cutver suggested dropping the commit option; if you then tried to continue
  that publication, the same program would not allow it. The message now explains what each path does.
- **Less duplicated work when continuing a publication** ([#398](https://github.com/cutver/cutver/pull/398)):
  the plugin list used to be loaded twice; now once.
- **A plugin can no longer exhaust the program's memory with a huge output** ([#378](https://github.com/cutver/cutver/pull/378)):
  its answer is capped at 1 MiB and its error messages at 64 KiB, and the program keeps reading so it can say
  "too much output" instead of "took too long".
- **A failed publication no longer leaves child processes running** ([#388](https://github.com/cutver/cutver/pull/388)):
  on Windows the whole process tree is closed with one system call, instead of process by process.
- **`env("NAME", "default")` now works** ([#385](https://github.com/cutver/cutver/pull/385)): it was
  documented with two arguments, and the published version refused it.
- **A plugin's environment permissions are resolved when it runs**
  ([#366](https://github.com/cutver/cutver/pull/366)), **a busy external command no longer makes a
  publication fail at random** ([#379](https://github.com/cutver/cutver/pull/379)), and **`doctor` reports the
  permissions it actually found** ([#364](https://github.com/cutver/cutver/pull/364)).

The rest of the range between alpha.1 and this version is internal: the alpha's own release notes, a rule
about the documentation register, a proposed architecture decision, and records of work in progress. One
change there is worth naming because it is real and it is this repository's own: the release hooks in
`cutver.toml` were bounded by a timeout, since an absent one means no bound at all
([#405](https://github.com/cutver/cutver/pull/405)). None of it changes what cutver does on your machine.

## What this version does not include

- **It is a beta, so the publishing process is still what is being tested.** The ladder is alpha.1 → beta.1 →
  rc.1 → 0.22.0, and only at the last stage is 0.22.0 the version to install for real work. If something
  fails here, treat it as a failure of the publishing process until proven otherwise.
- **This repository's gate path has not been exercised by a real release yet.** The configuration, the
  `attest` job and the download are in the tree, and the workflow's job graph is pinned by a test
  (`tests/release_pipeline_contract.rs`), but the first run of that path is the publication these notes
  describe — a dispatch that has not happened when they were written. Nothing here proves it works.
- **There is no guide for wiring `[gates] require` into a workflow.** The reference pages state the flags,
  the file shape and the configuration table, and the commit that wired this repository's own pipeline
  records two traps an operator hits — uploading a hidden directory needs `include-hidden-files`, and the
  workflow's own contract test pins the publishing job's `needs:` line
  ([ADR-0006](https://github.com/cutver/cutver/blob/main/docs/adr/0006-progressive-onboarding-and-composable-primitives.md)).
  Neither is discoverable from the reference alone, which is the gap.
- **A required gate is enforced at publish, not at bump.** `bump --defer-publish` does not consult the gate
  store, so a `[gates] require` with no attestation step is not noticed until the publication job refuses —
  after the release branch was pushed.
- **The container image tag set and the package-manager entries were not checked** when these notes were
  written: the access used to write them cannot read published packages. What each should contain is fixed
  by the automated tests, but it was not observed in practice.
- **The notice about the skipped moving tag is a line of the plan tree.** `plan` and `publish` print it and
  `bump` does not. `publish --json` prints no tree at all, so the same fact is there as `floating_tag: null`.
- **`init --dry-run` does not exist.** `--json` landed ahead of it, and the proposal that asks for both
  remains `proposed` with its rules unstarted
  ([ADR-0006](https://github.com/cutver/cutver/blob/main/docs/adr/0006-progressive-onboarding-and-composable-primitives.md)).
  That is a proposal, not a commitment for the next release.
- **Two items of the general plan are still open**
  ([#326](https://github.com/cutver/cutver/issues/326), gaps 8 and 9): declaring what each stage needs, and
  passing the project folder on the command line. Nothing in either layer of these notes touches them.
- **winget is not ready yet.** The one-package-per-manager decision covers Scoop and Homebrew. winget is a new
  destination with its own review process, and it is not in this version.

## Documentation

- [Command reference](https://github.com/cutver/cutver/blob/main/docs/reference/cli.md#cutver-bump) — the
  channel ladder under `bump`, and the `--json` rows on `publish`, `attest` and `init`.
- [The release tail's three machine surfaces](https://github.com/cutver/cutver/blob/main/docs/internals/machine-contract-release-tail.md)
  — every key of the three objects, the file the record lands in, and what a consumer does with each.
- [Resuming a closing phase](https://github.com/cutver/cutver/blob/main/docs/internals/release-resume.md) —
  what a resume repeats, what it refuses, and the evidence each refusal names.
- [Publishing, and continuing a publication](https://github.com/cutver/cutver/blob/main/docs/internals/pipeline.md#two-phase-release-prepare-verify-publish)
  — the closing steps, what can be repeated, and the case that cannot be recovered.
- [The machine contract](https://github.com/cutver/cutver/blob/main/docs/internals/machine-contract.md#surfaces)
  — the index of the surfaces that answer with `schemaVersion`, and the error envelope they share.
- [Installing cutver](https://github.com/cutver/cutver/blob/main/docs/guides/installation.md#installing-cutver)
  — one package per manager, and where to find the lean version.
- [Writing a plugin](https://github.com/cutver/cutver/blob/main/docs/guides/plugin-authoring.md#writing-a-plugin)
  — the protocol version, and the environment a child process receives.
- [The process runtime](https://github.com/cutver/cutver/blob/main/docs/guides/plugin-process-runtime.md#how-command-is-resolved)
  — how a process plugin's `command` resolves and the working directory it runs in, which is the workspace
  root since the change in #368.
